opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the first thing to understand is how FrontierMath is structured. The problems aren't uniform in difficulty. There's a spread: some are roughly at the level of a strong undergraduate or an early graduate student who knows the relevant area, some are at the level where you'd want a researcher who specializes in that subfield, and then there's a top tier that would take even experts a substantial amount of time and effort to work through. So when you say 75%, you're not saying the model has solved everything, including the hardest research-flavored problems. You're saying it has cleared most of the lower and middle tiers and made decent inroads into the hard stuff.

And when I look at the trajectory of these models, that seems quite plausible to me. When we first released the benchmark, the best models were scoring in the low single digits, and people took that as a sign that the benchmark would hold up for a long time. But then reasoning models came along, the ones trained with reinforcement learning to think for a long time before answering, and scores jumped quite dramatically within a matter of months. That tells you a few things. One is that a lot of what makes these problems hard for models isn't some deep, unbridgeable gap in mathematical insight. It's things like being able to carry out a long chain of computation without making errors, knowing the relevant literature and techniques, and being willing to try many approaches and check your work. Those are exactly the things that more inference compute and better RL training improve.

The other thing is that our problems are designed to have definite, automatically verifiable answers, usually a specific number or object. That's important for grading, but it also means the problems are somewhat amenable to the kind of approach where you explore, compute, sanity-check, and converge on an answer. Models are getting very good at that loop.

So 75% is impressive in the sense that it would mean the model is doing mathematics that most professional mathematicians outside the specific subfield couldn't do quickly. But it's reasonable in the sense that I don't think it requires anything qualitatively new beyond continued scaling of the current paradigm. What I'd be more cautious about is reading too much into it. Solving well-posed problems with known answers is a different skill from what research mathematicians spend most of their time doing, which is figuring out what the right questions are, building up new frameworks, and working on things for months or years where you don't even know if there's a clean answer. A high FrontierMath score doesn't directly tell you a model can do that. So I'd say it's a meaningful signal of capability, but it's not the same thing as automating mathematical research.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the first thing to say is that when we built FrontierMath, we deliberately tried to make it hard. The problems range from things that a strong undergraduate or early graduate student could do with a few hours of effort, all the way up to research-level problems that even specialists in the relevant subfield would find challenging. So when models first came out and were scoring, you know, two percent, that felt roughly consistent with the difficulty we were going for.

But I think people sometimes overinterpret what a benchmark like this measures. A lot of the problems, especially in the lower tiers, are really about knowing the right technique and executing it carefully, maybe with a bit of computation along the way. That's exactly the kind of thing that models have been getting dramatically better at, because you can train on it with reinforcement learning when you have verifiable answers. And FrontierMath has numerical, automatically checkable answers by design, so it's actually quite a natural target for that kind of training.

So if you ask me whether 75% is plausible in the near term, I'd say yes, and I don't think it requires some fundamental breakthrough. The trend on math benchmarks has been that each one gets saturated faster than people expected. GSM8K, then MATH, then competition-level problems like AIME. FrontierMath is harder than those, but it's harder in a way that's mostly continuous with them, not a totally different kind of task.

The caveat I'd add is that the top tier of problems, the ones that are genuinely research-adjacent, I'd expect to remain more resistant. So you might see a model get to 75% overall while still struggling on the hardest fifteen or twenty percent. And that's an important distinction, because the question people actually care about is whether these systems can do novel mathematics, and a high aggregate score doesn't fully answer that. Still, going from two percent to three quarters on a benchmark that mathematicians thought was quite hard, that's a real capability gain, and I think it's a reasonable thing to expect rather than a wild prediction.

astra-6.text:
Well, I think it’s useful to separate how difficult the problems are from how confident we should be that AI systems can eventually solve them. FrontierMath is meant to test advanced mathematical reasoning, so getting 75% would be impressive. It would mean solving a broad range of difficult problems reliably, rather than just producing a few striking examples.

But difficulty for humans doesn’t necessarily imply that these problems will remain out of reach for AI. A model can make progress by combining mathematical knowledge with longer reasoning, trying different approaches, and checking intermediate results. If those capabilities keep improving, then 75% seems like a reasonable prospect, even though it would represent a substantial advance.

I’d also distinguish that from saying the system could do all the work of a research mathematician. Solving a precisely stated problem is one thing; choosing fruitful questions and developing new mathematical ideas is a broader task. So it would be a significant result without necessarily settling the question of whether AI can automate mathematical research.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, FrontierMath consists of original problems that can take expert mathematicians hours or even days to solve. So getting 75% would be a substantial achievement. You need to find an approach, work through a long argument, and check that your answer is correct. It’s much more demanding than applying a familiar formula.

But the problems were selected to be solvable. They’re not famous open problems that have resisted decades of effort. We know there are solutions within reach of human experts, so there’s no obvious reason sufficiently capable AI systems couldn’t find them too.

That’s why I’d distinguish impressive from implausible. A score like that would demonstrate a lot of mathematical problem-solving ability, but it wouldn’t automatically mean the system could do every aspect of mathematical research, like choosing fruitful questions or developing new theories.
